entities.name: Mark of Toledo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mark of Toledo (Marcus Toletanus), a Spanish physician and canon, emerged as a pivotal figure in the intellectual landscape of early 13th-century Iberia, contributing significantly to the transmission of Arabic knowledge into Latin Europe. Active within the renowned Toledo School of Translators, his career, culminating in his death on April 18, 1226, was defined by a profound engagement with both Islamic religious texts and classical Greek scientific and philosophical works preserved in Arabic. His efforts were instrumental in bridging the cultural and linguistic divides between the Islamic and Christian worlds, albeit often with polemical intent in the case of religious texts, during a period of intense intellectual ferment and geopolitical tension across the Iberian Peninsula.

His most celebrated and impactful contribution was the complete Latin translation of the Qur'an, completed around 1210. This rendition, often referred to as the 'Lex Mahumet pseudoprophete,' was not intended for interfaith dialogue but rather to equip Christian theologians with the means to understand and refute Islamic doctrine, a common motivation during the Reconquista and the Crusades. Beyond theology, Mark of Toledo was a prolific translator of medical and philosophical texts, rendering works by Galen, Hippocrates, and Avicenna from Arabic into Latin. His translations of Galen's 'De motibus dubiis' and 'De pulsibus ad tirones,' alongside other medical treatises, provided Latin scholars with crucial access to advanced medical knowledge that had been lost to Western Europe for centuries, significantly impacting the development of medieval European medicine.
